title: Barbed Wire Sunday: Berlin Divided Overnight
subtitle: The sealing of the Berlin sector border, 13 August 1961, through the Checkpoint Charlie standoff of 27–28 October 1961
intro: In the early hours of Sunday 13 August 1961, East German police, soldiers and factory militia unrolled barbed wire along the 43-kilometre line between East and West Berlin and tore up streets at the crossings. Trains and trams stopped at the sector boundary. By breakfast the two halves of a city that had shared underground lines, workplaces and families were cut apart, and over the following days the wire was replaced by concrete blocks and bricked-up house fronts. Two months earlier Walter Ulbricht had told a press conference that no one intended to build a wall.

Very little of this chapter's record is diary. The first weeks were written down mostly by institutions: the Stasi's secret reports to the leadership on how the population was reacting, the East Berlin police journal logging crowds and escapes entry by entry, a transport-police report on the first fatal shooting, and on the Western side a mayor's letter, a President's reply, a Vice President's report and a general's telegrams, which the US Foreign Relations series has since published. Around them stand open letters between writers on both sides, newspaper headlines, a photograph, and accounts by survivors' families written down decades later. Each entry is labelled for what it is.

The GDR's own position is given in its own documents. The Council of Ministers presented the closure as the ordinary border control of a sovereign state against espionage, the luring away of workers and West German militarism, and the barrier later received the official name 'antifaschistischer Schutzwall'. Stephan Hermlin argued that Berlin had been divided since 1948. The Western positions are given in theirs: Brandt called the closure the most serious encroachment since the blockade and feared a ghetto; Kennedy wrote that only war could reverse it and chose to reinforce West Berlin instead; and the West Berlin press accused the allies of doing nothing. Western rights in West Berlin and Western access were the lines the United States had said it would defend, and those were not crossed.

Between the papers are people. Conrad Schumann, a 19-year-old policeman, jumped the wire on the third day. Ida Siekmann, 58, jumped from her window on Bernauer Straße on 22 August and died. Günter Litfin, 24, was shot in the water of the Humboldthafen on 24 August. Neither victim left words of their own, and they appear here only through what others recorded; their deaths are given soberly, as the records give them, and with the gap between the police log's few lines and the newspapers' headlines left visible.

Some expected voices are missing. No diary entry by Brigitte Reimann about 13 August 1961 was found in the sources checked; her diary is represented by an earlier entry on her brother's departure to the West. Christa Wolf's 'Ein Tag im Jahr' contains an entry for 27 September 1961, from the years when she lived in Halle and was gathering the material for 'Der geteilte Himmel', but its text could not be checked and it is not summarised here. The private diaries of ordinary Berliners held by the Berlin Wall Foundation are also not represented, because their published texts were not reached. The chapter closes in October, when Soviet and American tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie over who had the right to cross the line.
seam: These records show a border made real by agreement on one side and refusal on the other: a decree that called the line the ordinary frontier of a sovereign state, and Western notes that called it illegal while promising only to defend what lay behind it. A police log wrote down a jump from No. 48 as a line among crowd counts, while the papers across the street named Ida Siekmann. Writers who had been colleagues argued about whether the city had already been divided before the wire. As in The City & the City, the hardest part of the border was learning not to see the people on the other side of it.

eyes.name: SED leadership, GDR Council of Ministers and the party press (Neues Deutschland)
eyes.role: Ruling party and state of the German Democratic Republic; Walter Ulbricht was SED First Secretary and Chairman of the Council of State; Neues Deutschland was the party's central newspaper
eyes.where: East Berlin: government buildings in the city centre
eyes.form: official records, press conference transcript, newspaper
eyes.authenticity: Ulbricht's 15 June 1961 press-conference answer is printed in Dokumente zur Deutschlandpolitik, Reihe IV, Bd. 6 (1975), and reproduced by the Chronik der Mauer. The Council of Ministers decision of 12 August 1961 is reproduced by German History in Documents and Images (GHDI). Neues Deutschland coverage is summarised here from secondary descriptions, not read in full.
eyes.bio: The SED leadership planned the border closure, code-named in Stasi files as 'Aktion Rose', with Soviet consent. Its own records present the measure as a defence against Western 'agents', 'head-hunters' and militarism, later fixed in the official name 'antifaschistischer Schutzwall'. These documents are the GDR's case in its own words.

sources.title: Ulbricht press conference, 15 June 1961 (Chronik der Mauer PDF)
GHDI: Walter Ulbricht's speech on the Berlin question, 15 June 1961
GHDI: Building the Berlin Wall, 13 August 1961 (with related documents)

eyes.name: Ministry for State Security (MfS), Central Evaluation and Information Group (ZAIG)
eyes.role: The GDR secret police's reporting office, which sent daily situation reports to the SED leadership
eyes.where: MfS headquarters, Normannenstraße, East Berlin-Lichtenberg, compiling reports from across the GDR
eyes.vantage_label: the state listening to its own people
eyes.authenticity: Held by the Bundesarchiv (former BStU), e.g. BArch, MfS, ZAIG, Nr. 31066; twelve reports on 'Aktion Rose' up to 16 August 1961, several published on the Stasi-Mediathek and in the edition 'Die DDR im Blick der Stasi 1961'. The Bundesarchiv cautions that reported approval often came from SED agitation teams.
eyes.bio: The Stasi wrote for an audience of a few leaders who wanted to know whether the population would accept the closure. Its reports record crowds, strikes, absences and angry remarks, alongside approval it partly manufactured. It is the nearest thing the record has to a daily diary of East German reactions, kept by those whose job was watching.

sources.title: Bundesarchiv: Der Mauerbau in den Unterlagen der Staatssicherheit, II. Berichte an die Staatsführung
Stasi-Mediathek: Erster Bericht über die Aktion 'Rose'
Stasi-Mediathek: Dritte Einzel-Information über die Durchführung der Aktion 'Rose' (dok805, PDF)
Die DDR im Blick der Stasi: Jahrgang 1961

eyes.name: East Berlin police logs: Präsidium der Volkspolizei and Transportpolizei
eyes.role: The operations staff of the East Berlin People's Police and the railway Transport Police section, logging events on the new sector border hour by hour
eyes.where: Police Presidium, Keibelstraße, East Berlin; posts along the sector border
eyes.authenticity: Typed copies in the Landesarchiv Berlin (C Rep. 303/26.1/239 and Transportpolizei records), published as PDFs by the Chronik der Mauer with spelling corrected and personal data of private persons anonymised.
eyes.bio: The 'Journal der Handlung' is a running log, entry by numbered entry, of what the police saw across the line: crowds, cameras, loudspeaker vans, escapes. It records people leaping from windows in the same flat tone as motorcades. The Transportpolizei report on Günter Litfin is the shooters' own account of the first death by gunfire.

sources.title: PdVP Journal der Handlung, 22 August 1961 (Chronik der Mauer PDF)
Transportpolizei report on Günter Litfin, 24 August 1961 (Chronik der Mauer PDF)

eyes.name: Hans Conrad Schumann
eyes.role: Aged 19; a non-commissioned officer of the East German Bereitschaftspolizei (barracked police) posted to guard the barbed wire at Bernauer Straße
eyes.where: Corner of Ruppiner Straße and Bernauer Straße
eyes.authenticity: No diary. The jump is fixed by Peter Leibing's photograph of 15 August 1961 and contemporary film; Schumann's own accounts were given in interviews years later. The Deutsches Historisches Museum's 2021 installation 'The Leap – 1961' gives the time and place.
eyes.bio: Schumann was one of the young police set to hold the line in its first days, when it was still coils of wire. His leap became the most reproduced image of the wall's beginning. He settled in Bavaria and died in 1998.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum: The Leap – 1961

eyes.name: Ida Siekmann
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. Aged 58; living alone at Bernauer Straße 48, a house on the East Berlin side whose front pavement belonged to West Berlin; her sister lived a few streets away in the West
eyes.form: recorded by others (police log, press, memorial research)
eyes.authenticity: She left no known writing about these days. Her death is reconstructed by the Chronik der Mauer / Berlin Wall Foundation biography (Christine Brecht) from West Berlin newspapers of 23 August 1961 and an East Berlin police report (PdVP-Rapport Nr. 234, 23 August 1961).
eyes.bio: Siekmann's house became part of the border itself: its doors on to the street were bricked up, but its windows still opened over West Berlin pavement. She is counted as the first person known to have died at the wall. She is included here only through what others recorded.

sources.title: Chronik der Mauer: Ida Siekmann

eyes.name: Günter Litfin (and his brother Jürgen Litfin)
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. Aged 24; a tailor from Weißensee in East Berlin who had worked in West Berlin until the border closed on 13 August. His younger brother Jürgen later wrote the family's account
eyes.where: Humboldthafen, by the Charité, on the sector line between Mitte and Tiergarten
eyes.form: recorded by others; brother's later memoir
eyes.authenticity: Günter Litfin left no account. The shooting is documented by the Transportpolizei report of 24 August 1961, East and West press of 25–26 August, a 1997 Berlin court verdict, and Jürgen Litfin's book 'Tod durch fremde Hand' (2006).
eyes.bio: Litfin was the first person shot dead at the Berlin border under the order to fire. The East Berlin press blackened his name; his family were told to keep silent and learned of his death from West Berlin television. Decades later his brother turned a former border watchtower into a memorial.

sources.title: Chronik der Mauer: Günter Litfin
Berlin Wall Foundation: Günter Litfin Memorial

eyes.name: Willy Brandt
eyes.role: Aged 47; Governing Mayor of West Berlin and SPD candidate for Chancellor in the federal election of 17 September 1961
eyes.side: West Berlin / Federal Republic of Germany (SPD)
eyes.where: West Berlin: Rathaus Schöneberg; the sector border
eyes.authenticity: The letter of 16 August 1961 to Kennedy survives in an informal US translation telegraphed by the Berlin Mission (FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 117); the German original is reproduced by the Chronik der Mauer. Speeches are summarised from secondary descriptions.
eyes.bio: Brandt had to speak for a city that could do nothing by force and depended on allies who were moving slowly. His letter to Kennedy is blunt about the danger of Western passivity. His experience of these weeks fed his later policy of small steps toward the East.

sources.title: FRUS 1961–63 XIV, doc. 117: Telegram from the Mission at Berlin (Brandt's letter)
Brandt to Kennedy, 16 August 1961 (Chronik der Mauer PDF)

eyes.name: John F. Kennedy
eyes.role: Aged 44; President of the United States
eyes.where: Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, on 13 August; the White House thereafter
eyes.authenticity: The reply to Brandt of 18 August 1961 is FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 120 (Kennedy Library, printed from an unsigned copy); US-government text. The private remark about the wall is known only from Kenneth O'Donnell and David Powers, 'Johnny, We Hardly Knew Ye' (1972).
eyes.bio: Kennedy's red lines in July 1961 had been Western presence, access and the freedom of West Berlin, not East Berlin. The closure crossed none of them, and his letters and reported remarks show relief mixed with the need to reassure. His reply to Brandt is the clearest statement of that position.

sources.title: FRUS 1961–63 XIV, doc. 120: Letter from President Kennedy to Governing Mayor Brandt
Kennedy to Brandt, 18 August 1961 (Chronik der Mauer PDF)

eyes.name: Lyndon B. Johnson
eyes.role: Aged 52; Vice President of the United States, sent by Kennedy to Bonn and West Berlin, 19–20 August 1961
eyes.authenticity: His report on the trip is FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 121 ('Washington, undated'); US-government text. The Schöneberg speech is known from news reports and film.
eyes.bio: Johnson was sent as a symbol, carrying Kennedy's reply to Brandt and meeting the reinforcements on the road in. His report measures Berlin's mood in crowds and cheers. It is candid that tanks drew louder cheers than words.

sources.title: FRUS 1961–63 XIV, doc. 121: Report by Vice President Johnson

eyes.name: Lucius D. Clay
eyes.role: Aged 63; retired general, former military governor of the US zone and hero of the 1948–49 airlift; accompanied Johnson in August and returned in September as Kennedy's personal representative in Berlin
eyes.where: West Berlin (US headquarters, Dahlem); Friedrichstraße crossing in October
eyes.authenticity: His message of 27 October 1961 to Secretary Rusk was sent through the Berlin Mission (FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 195); the standoff is summarised in FRUS editorial note doc. 196. US-government texts.
eyes.bio: Clay wanted to test Soviet responsibility for East Berlin by sending US officials through the crossing and refusing to show papers to East German police. The test produced the tank standoff of 27–28 October. His telegrams show the Western insistence on the old four-power agreement at the point where it met the new line.

sources.title: FRUS 1961–63 XIV, doc. 195: Telegram from the Mission at Berlin, 27 October 1961
FRUS 1961–63 XIV, doc. 196: Editorial Note on the tank confrontation

eyes.name: Günter Grass (with Wolfdietrich Schnurre)
eyes.role: Aged 33; West Berlin novelist, author of 'Die Blechtrommel' (1959)
eyes.authenticity: The open letter of Grass and Schnurre to East German writers (16 August 1961) and the replies were collected that year in Hans Werner Richter (ed.), 'Die Mauer oder Der 13. August' (Rowohlt, 1961).
eyes.bio: Grass and Schnurre wrote across the new line to colleagues in the East, asking them to say where they stood. The exchange is one of the few dated, public conversations between Germans on the two sides in the first week. It shows writers who had shared stages a month earlier now arguing through the press.

sources.title: Hermlin's reply to Schnurre and Grass, 17 August 1961 (Chronik der Mauer PDF; cites the Richter volume)

eyes.name: Stephan Hermlin
eyes.role: Aged 45; East Berlin poet and essayist, a communist who had been in exile and fought in Spain
eyes.authenticity: Open letter dated Berlin, 17 August 1961, printed in Richter (ed.), 'Die Mauer oder Der 13. August' (1961), pp. 66–68; copy published by the Chronik der Mauer.
eyes.bio: Hermlin answered Grass and Schnurre within a day. His letter gives the GDR position as a writer argued it, not as a decree: Berlin was already divided, and the West had no right to lecture. It sits beside the Western letters as the other half of one exchange.

sources.title: Stephan Hermlin, open letter, 17 August 1961 (Chronik der Mauer PDF)

eyes.name: Brigitte Reimann
eyes.role: Aged 26–27; East German novelist, working at the brown-coal combine 'Schwarze Pumpe' and living in Hoyerswerda
eyes.vantage_label: same country, a family already split
eyes.authenticity: Diaries published as 'Ich bedaure nichts. Tagebücher 1955–1963' (Aufbau, 1997). An entry of 29 April 1960 is excerpted on panel 16 of the Brigitte Reimann exhibition. An entry about 13 August 1961 could not be found in the sources checked for this chapter.
eyes.bio: Reimann's brother Lutz left for the West in 1960, more than a year before the border closed. Her diary records that loss as the split of a family between 'our two Germanys'. She turned it into the novel 'Die Geschwister' (1963), which appeared the same year as Christa Wolf's 'Der geteilte Himmel'.

sources.title: Brigitte Reimann exhibition, panel 16 (PDF)

eyes.name: West Berlin, West German and American press (Bild, B.Z., Berliner Morgenpost, TIME)
eyes.role: Newspapers and magazines reporting from and to the Western side
eyes.side: West Berlin / Federal Republic / United States
eyes.authenticity: Headlines as cited by the Konrad Adenauer Foundation (Bild, 16 August 1961) and by the Chronik der Mauer victim biographies (B.Z., Berliner Morgenpost, Bild, Frankfurter Rundschau, Frankfurter Allgemeine, 23–26 August 1961); TIME, 25 August 1961, 'Berlin: The Wall', read in part.
eyes.bio: The Western press was both witness and actor: it photographed the wire, named the dead and accused the Western allies of doing nothing. Its anger at Bonn, London and Washington is as much a part of the record as its anger at the East.

sources.title: Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung / Stiftung Bundeskanzler-Adenauer-Haus: Mauerbau 1961 (PDF)
TIME, 25 August 1961: 'Berlin: The Wall'

entries.headline: A brother goes West, and a family splits
entries.digest: Reimann notes that her brother Lutz has left for the West with his wife and baby. She sees her own family now divided between the two German states. She writes that this tragedy of the two Germanys is a subject no one has yet made into a lasting book. Sixteen months later the same split would be fixed in concrete for millions.
entries.source_note: Excerpt quoted on Brigitte Reimann exhibition panel 16 (TBI, entry dated 29.04.1960); diaries published as 'Ich bedaure nichts' (1997).

entries.headline: Ulbricht: 'No one intends to build a wall'
entries.digest: Asked by Annamarie Doherr of the Frankfurter Rundschau whether a state border would be set up at the Brandenburg Gate, Ulbricht answered at length about a peace treaty and West Berlin as a 'free city'. In the middle he said that no one had the intention of erecting a wall, and that the building workers were busy with housing. No one had asked about a wall; the word came from him. Two months later the border was closed.
entries.quote: Niemand hat die Absicht, eine Mauer zu errichten.
entries.source_note: Transcript in Dokumente zur Deutschlandpolitik IV/6 (1975), pp. 925 ff., reproduced by Chronik der Mauer (PDF 56682). World-famous phrase.

entries.headline: The decision to seal the border is signed
entries.digest: The GDR Council of Ministers resolved to impose on the borders with West Berlin the kind of control usual at the frontier of a sovereign state. The text presented the measure as protection against West German 'revanchism', espionage and the 'trade in people' that drew workers westward. It followed a Warsaw Pact request that the GDR act. The measures were to take effect that night.
entries.source_note: GHDI lists 'GDR Council of Ministers' Decision to Seal the Border (August 12, 1961)' among the documents for 13 August 1961; content summarised from the published decree.

entries.headline: First report on 'Aktion Rose': the transport police were late
entries.digest: The Stasi's first report to the leadership said the operation had gone broadly to plan, but that the deployment of the Transportpolizei at the railway stations failed because it was wrongly timed. A second report hours later said the Stasi had carried out most of the station measures itself. Another report describes East Germans returning from West Berlin being held up at Mahlow around 3 a.m., until orders came to let them through.
entries.source_note: Bundesarchiv, 'Berichte an die Staatsführung'; Stasi-Mediathek, Erster Bericht über die Aktion 'Rose', Bl. 353 (BArch, MfS, ZAIG, Nr. 31066).

entries.headline: The party paper announces the measures as protection
entries.digest: Neues Deutschland's Sunday issue carried the Warsaw Pact states' declaration and the Council of Ministers decision. Readers learned that the border to West Berlin was now under control and that East Berliners would need special permission to cross. The measures were framed as a defence of peace against West German militarism, not as a barrier against the GDR's own people.
entries.source_note: Summarised from the published decree and declaration (GHDI); the ND issue itself was not consulted for this chapter.

entries.date_display: Sunday 13 August 1961, later in the day
entries.headline: Crowds gather; the Stasi counts more yes than no
entries.digest: Early reports described calm at the crossings. Later the same day the Stasi recorded groups of 50 to 100 people gathering, some openly criticising the measures, and 20 to 30 at Friedrichstraße station. Remarks it logged compared the day to 17 June 1953, and one used the word 'KZ', concentration camp. The last report of the day nevertheless judged that positive statements outweighed negative ones. The Bundesarchiv notes that much of the approval came from SED agitation teams.
entries.source_note: Bundesarchiv, 'Berichte an die Staatsführung' (five reports on 13 August).

entries.headline: What the West is saying, as the Stasi heard it
entries.digest: A Stasi report on Western reactions found that Bonn, the West Berlin Senate and the Western powers were calling for protests but warning against rash steps. It attributed to the US city commandant, Albert Watson, a remark that the closure was only a traffic disruption. The remark is known here only through the Stasi's report of it.
entries.source_note: Stasi-Mediathek, 'Bericht über westliche Reaktionen nach dem Mauerbau', Bl. 122; summarised by the Bundesarchiv, which gives no exact date for this report within 13–15 August.

entries.headline: The mayor protests to the world, and asks for calm
entries.digest: Brandt had travelled overnight from his election campaign. Before a special session of the West Berlin parliament he denounced the closure as unlawful and inhuman. He called on the Western powers to act against it and told Berliners on both sides not to let themselves be provoked. The speech had to do two things at once: give voice to anger and keep anger from turning to violence at the wire.
entries.source_note: Summarised from general accounts of the special session; the speech text was not consulted for this chapter.

entries.headline: Monday at the factories: absences, a strike, a resolution
entries.digest: On the first working day, the Stasi reported that attendance at VEB Bergmann-Borsig was about 60 percent, partly blamed on broken transport. A concrete plant in Berlin-Grünau drafted a resolution against the measures, and workers at VEB Holzbau in Oranienburg struck to demand their reversal. At VEB Kühlautomat a party secretary was attacked after a discussion, and youths in Hennigsdorf talked of breaking through the border. The reports also noted that the Western powers seemed unwilling to challenge the closure.
entries.source_note: Bundesarchiv, 'Berichte an die Staatsführung' (four reports on 14 August); the article lists these incidents without assigning each to a precise day.

entries.headline: An open letter to Anna Seghers
entries.digest: Grass addressed the chair of the GDR Writers' Union, Anna Seghers, an author he admired. He asked her to speak against the tanks and wire as she had once spoken against fascism. The letter put a moral question to a single named person on the other side.
entries.source_note: Collected in H. W. Richter (ed.), 'Die Mauer oder Der 13. August' (1961); date and content not checked against the text for this chapter.

entries.place: Corner of Ruppiner Straße and Bernauer Straße
entries.headline: A young guard jumps the wire
entries.digest: At about four in the afternoon, Schumann, standing guard on a stretch where the border was still a low roll of barbed wire, ran and leapt over it into West Berlin. Peter Leibing, a young photographer, caught him in mid-air. The picture of a guard of the new border leaving it within three days travelled round the world.
entries.source_note: Deutsches Historisches Museum, 'The Leap – 1961' (time, place, photographer). Schumann's own accounts date from later interviews.

entries.headline: Brandt and the commandants agree: no provocation
entries.digest: A Stasi report told the leadership that Willy Brandt had agreed with the Western city commandants to avoid any provocation from West Berlin. The same day the three Western commandants delivered a written protest to their Soviet counterpart. Read together, the two show the GDR learning that the West would protest but not tear down the wire.
entries.source_note: Bundesarchiv, 'Berichte an die Staatsführung'; Stasi-Mediathek, Dritte Einzel-Information, Bl. 344 (dated 13 August on the Mediathek page, cited for 15 August in the Bundesarchiv article). Commandants' protest date from general accounts.

entries.headline: Bild: 'The West does NOTHING!'
entries.digest: The mass-circulation Bild ran the headline 'Der Westen tut NICHTS!' across its front page. It voiced a feeling that the allies had left Berlin to its fate, three days after the wire went up. The same day, a crowd put at about 250,000 gathered before the Rathaus Schöneberg.
entries.source_note: Headline and crowd figure as given by the Stiftung Bundeskanzler-Adenauer-Haus, 'Mauerbau 1961' (PDF). Famous headline.

entries.headline: A letter to Kennedy: the most serious encroachment since the blockade
entries.digest: Brandt wrote directly to the President. He argued that the East German measures, backed by Moscow, had nearly destroyed what was left of four-power status in Berlin, and that passivity would damage Western credibility and embolden East Berlin. He asked for a reaffirmation of Western presence, a United Nations move and a visible reinforcement of the American garrison. He warned that West Berlin could become a ghetto cut off from the Federal Republic.
entries.quote: I regard this encroachment as the most serious in the postwar history of this city since the blockade.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 117 (informal US translation telegraphed by the Berlin Mission, 16 August 1961, midnight). US-government text.

entries.place: West Berlin, before the Rathaus Schöneberg
entries.headline: Speaking to a quarter of a million
entries.digest: Brandt addressed the protest crowd in front of the city hall. He told Berliners that the city expected more than words from its allies, and he spoke directly to the East Berlin police not to fire on their own people. Placards in the crowd demanded that Kennedy come to Berlin.
entries.source_note: Rally and size: Stiftung Bundeskanzler-Adenauer-Haus PDF; placards: TIME, 25 August 1961. Speech content from general accounts, not from the text.

entries.headline: Grass and Schnurre write to the writers of the East
entries.digest: Together with Wolfdietrich Schnurre, Grass sent an open letter to the members of the GDR Writers' Union. It asked them to say publicly whether they approved of the closure of the border and the troops at it. The letter treated silence as a position in itself.
entries.source_note: Date and addressees from Hermlin's reply of 17 August (Chronik der Mauer PDF 58832); content summarised from that reply's framing.

entries.headline: Hermlin answers: Berlin was divided long ago
entries.digest: Hermlin rejected the premise that 13 August was an injustice. Berlin, he argued, had been split since the 1948 currency reform, with two currencies, two police forces and two social systems, and Western rights in West Berlin were untouched. He gave his government his serious, unqualified support, saying the measures checked an aggressive West German state. He recalled 1933 and asked where the Western defenders of freedom had been, while saying that he still favoured free travel.
entries.source_note: Hermlin to Schnurre and Grass, Berlin, 17 August 1961; Richter (ed.), 'Die Mauer oder Der 13. August' (1961), pp. 66–68; Chronik der Mauer PDF 58832.

entries.headline: Kennedy to Brandt: only war could reverse this
entries.digest: Kennedy replied that the border closing was a basic Soviet decision which only war could undo. He agreed that the best immediate answer was a significant reinforcement of the Western garrisons. He announced that Johnson and General Clay were coming with authority to talk frankly.
entries.quote: this brutal border closing evidently represents a basic Soviet decision which only war could reverse.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 120 (Kennedy Library, printed from an unsigned copy). US-government text.

entries.headline: 'A wall is a hell of a lot better than a war'
entries.digest: According to his aides Kenneth O'Donnell and David Powers, Kennedy said privately in these weeks that the wall was not a nice solution but much better than war. The remark fits the logic of his letter to Brandt: Khrushchev had chosen to seal his own side instead of seizing West Berlin. It is known only from their memoir, written eleven years later.
entries.quote: a wall is a hell of a lot better than a war
entries.form: remark reported in a later memoir
entries.source_note: Kenneth P. O'Donnell and David F. Powers, 'Johnny, We Hardly Knew Ye' (1972). Exact date not given; placed here beside the letter. Widely quoted phrase.

entries.headline: Johnson pledges 'our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor'
entries.digest: After talks with Adenauer in Bonn, Johnson flew in with Clay and Kennedy's reply to Brandt. Before the West Berlin parliament and a vast crowd outside, he invoked the closing pledge of the Declaration of Independence on behalf of the American commitment to the city. Contemporary reports describe people weeping and cheering; one estimate put the crowd at 300,000.
entries.quote: our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor
entries.source_note: Speech as reported by period news summaries (realtime1960s compilation); Bundesarchiv photo of crowds greeting Johnson, 19 August 1961, via GHDI. Crowd estimate unverified.

entries.headline: The airlift general comes back
entries.digest: Clay arrived with Johnson. For West Berliners, he was the man of the 1948–49 airlift, and his presence was meant as a signal that the United States would hold the city as it had then. A month later he returned to stay as the President's personal representative.
entries.source_note: Kennedy's letter of 18 August (FRUS XIV, doc. 120) announces Johnson's and Clay's visit; Clay's later appointment from general accounts.

entries.headline: The battle group rolls in
entries.digest: About 1,500 soldiers of the 1st Battle Group, 18th Infantry, under Colonel Glover Johns, drove down the autobahn from Helmstedt through East German territory into West Berlin. Johnson greeted them. Johns telephoned the White House that the first reinforcements were across. The access route the West insisted on had been used and not blocked.
entries.source_note: Military.com profile of Col. Glover S. Johns Jr. (troop numbers, call to the White House); Johnson's report, FRUS XIV, doc. 121. Unit designation from general accounts (the profile names the 8th Infantry Division).

entries.headline: Johnson's report: morale restored, and louder for the tanks
entries.digest: Johnson told the President that West Berlin's morale had been shaken but was restored, and he credited the arriving troops. He found Brandt apologetic about his letter and ready to agree that West Berlin should do more for its own defence. He noticed that the crowd's enthusiasm rose when tank carriers passed.
entries.quote: was noticeably higher when a few tank carriers went by
entries.source_note: FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 121 ('Washington, undated'). US-government text.

entries.headline: Police log: a jump from the third floor of No. 48
entries.digest: Entry 435 of the East Berlin police journal recorded that at Bernauer Straße 48 belongings had been thrown from the third floor and a person had then jumped from the window. The person lay on the ground and was taken away by fire brigade and ambulance; the log marks the report as confirmed. The log describes the jumper as a man and gives no name and no outcome.
entries.source_note: PdVP Journal der Handlung, 22 August 1961, entry 435 (Landesarchiv Berlin, C Rep. 303/26.1/239; Chronik der Mauer PDF 58846).

entries.headline: Ida Siekmann jumps, and dies
entries.digest: Her front door had been barricaded. Siekmann threw her bedding and belongings out of her third-floor window and jumped toward the West Berlin pavement. West Berlin firemen could not catch her in their net. She died on the way to the Lazarus hospital, the day before her 59th birthday, and is counted as the first known death at the wall.
entries.form: reconstruction from press and police records
entries.source_note: Chronik der Mauer biography by Christine Brecht, citing Berliner Morgenpost, Bild and Frankfurter Rundschau of 23 August 1961 and PdVP-Rapport Nr. 234 of 23 August 1961.

entries.headline: Brandt at 9:25, Adenauer at 12:40, and more windows
entries.digest: The same journal logged the Western visitors watched from the East: Brandt at about 9:25 and Chancellor Adenauer between about 12:40 and 1 p.m., each with a motorcade. It recorded crowds of around 500 at Bernauer and Brunnenstraße, police posted at ten-metre intervals, film cameras at the Church of Reconciliation, and loudspeaker vans on the western side. In the evening it noted items thrown from windows at Bernauer Straße 3 or 4 and a person reaching the West, and a young woman injured jumping at No. 7 and taken away by the police.
entries.source_note: PdVP Journal der Handlung, 22 August 1961, entries 443, 448, 462 and others (Chronik der Mauer PDF 58846).

entries.headline: 'A fatal jump to freedom'
entries.digest: West Berlin papers led with Ida Siekmann's death and blamed the East German leadership. One called it a fatal jump to freedom. The same coverage criticised Adenauer for taking nine days to come to Berlin.
entries.source_note: As summarised in the Chronik der Mauer biography of Ida Siekmann (Berliner Morgenpost, Bild, Frankfurter Rundschau, 23 August 1961).

entries.headline: Transport police report: the 'border violator' sank
entries.digest: The Transportpolizei report states that their post on the railway bridge saw a man and called on him to stop five times. He ran down the embankment steps into the Humboldthafen and swam toward the western bank. Warning shots and a burst into the water ahead of him were followed by two aimed shots, and he went under. Some 250 people watched from the western side; the body was recovered at about 7:10 p.m. The report names him and calls the event a prevented border breakthrough. Its first page bears the initials 'EH', attributed to Erich Honecker.
entries.source_note: Transportpolizei, Abschnitt Berlin, report of 24 August 1961 (Landesarchiv Berlin; Chronik der Mauer PDF 58850).

entries.headline: Günter Litfin is shot in the water
entries.digest: Litfin, who had worked in West Berlin until the border closed, tried to swim across the harbour basin. He was hit in the head just short of the western quay. He was the first person shot dead at the Berlin border under the order to fire. In 1997 a Berlin court convicted two of those responsible of joint manslaughter and gave suspended sentences.
entries.form: reconstruction from police records, press and court verdict
entries.source_note: Chronik der Mauer biography of Günter Litfin (Transportpolizei and police reports; Landgericht Berlin verdict of 17 January 1997).

entries.headline: A brother arrested; the family hears the news from Western TV
entries.digest: Jürgen Litfin was arrested and interrogated through the night, and the family flat was searched. The family learned that Günter was dead from a West Berlin television broadcast. Authorities pressed them to stay silent, and their death notice spoke of a tragic accident.
entries.source_note: Chronik der Mauer biography, drawing on Jürgen Litfin, 'Tod durch fremde Hand' (2006), and interviews (2001, 2006).

entries.headline: The party press: 'shots disregarded'
entries.digest: Under the headline 'Schüsse missachtet' the East Berlin press reported that a man pursued for criminal behaviour had ignored warning shots. In the following days Neues Deutschland and the television commentator Karl-Eduard von Schnitzler disparaged Litfin by name. The official account turned the first fatal shooting into a police matter.
entries.source_note: Chronik der Mauer biography of Günter Litfin, citing Berliner Zeitung, 25 August 1961, and Neues Deutschland.

entries.headline: B.Z.: Ulbricht's guards are murderers
entries.digest: The West Berlin B.Z. called the border guards who shot Litfin murderers. A day later the Frankfurter Allgemeine condemned their brutal cold-bloodedness. Spontaneous protests followed and a banner was hung at the harbour.
entries.source_note: Chronik der Mauer biography of Günter Litfin (B.Z., 25 August 1961; FAZ, 26 August 1961).

entries.headline: TIME: three days without an answer
entries.digest: TIME described the Vopos finishing their barrier while Washington, London and Paris made no retaliation for three days and Macmillan went grouse shooting. It reported Adenauer's idea of cutting interzonal trade and the allied note that threatened nothing. It described West Berliners massing at the city hall with placards asking for Kennedy and scorning paper protests, and Brandt's bitter talk of a new Munich.
entries.source_note: TIME, 25 August 1961, 'Berlin: The Wall' (page 4 of 10 read).

entries.headline: An official funeral in the West
entries.digest: West Berlin gave Siekmann an official funeral. A wreath read that she had been deprived of freedom, and her sister, who lived a few streets away in the West, received official condolences. In September the Wedding district put up a memorial of three logs wrapped in barbed wire outside her house.
entries.source_note: Chronik der Mauer biography of Ida Siekmann (Berliner Morgenpost, 16 September 1961).

entries.headline: The official name: 'anti-fascist protective rampart'
entries.digest: In the GDR's official language the barrier was not a wall but the 'antifaschistischer Schutzwall'. The term presented the border as a shield against fascism, militarism and Western subversion, and made its eastward-facing guard posts invisible in speech. Ulbricht's June denial and this later name sit side by side in the record.
entries.source_note: Official GDR term, widely documented; first use and date not pinned down for this chapter.

entries.headline: Soviet tanks face American tanks
entries.digest: After days of US probes in which American officials refused to show papers to East German police, ten Soviet tanks advanced up Friedrichstraße and stopped opposite the American tanks behind Checkpoint Charlie. By midnight there were thirty. In the evening Clay told the press that the appearance of Soviet tanks showed who was really responsible in East Berlin.
entries.form: editorial note in an official documentary series
entries.source_note: FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 196 (Editorial Note).

entries.headline: Clay to Rusk: 'a new phase of the war of nerves'
entries.digest: In a message relayed through the Mission, Clay reported that the confrontation had been with Soviet tanks manned by Soviet troops, which he saw as the point of the exercise. After a call with the White House he agreed to halt further probes until Monday and to send only uniformed Americans into East Berlin in the meantime. US troops were on partial alert.
entries.quote: we are just in a new phase of the war of nerves
entries.source_note: FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 195 (Mission at Berlin to Department of State, 27 October 1961, 8 p.m., signed Lightner). US-government text.

entries.headline: A call to Clay, known from one source
entries.digest: Curtis Cates's history of the crisis, 'The Ides of August', reports that Kennedy telephoned Clay that evening. FRUS found no other record of the call. Robert Kennedy later said the President asked him to use a back channel to the Soviet official Georgi Bolshakov to get the tanks withdrawn.
entries.source_note: FRUS XIV, doc. 196, citing Cates, 'The Ides of August', pp. 485–486, and Peter Wyden, 'Wall', p. 266.

entries.headline: The Soviet tanks pull back first
entries.digest: At about half past ten in the morning, Berlin time, the Soviet tanks began withdrawing, and the American tanks followed. Khrushchev later wrote that he ordered the pullback to let the Americans save face; Robert Kennedy credited the back channel. FRUS states that neither account is confirmed or refuted by the documents it holds.
entries.form: editorial note in an official documentary series
entries.source_note: FRUS 1961–63, vol. XIV, doc. 196, citing 'Khrushchev Remembers: The Last Testament' and Wyden, 'Wall'.

Ulbricht says no one intends to build a wall

claims.written: same day, Stasi report to the leadership; approval largely came from party agitators

claims.written: same day, open letter, East Berlin; book form 1961

convergences.label: Barbed Wire Sunday
convergences.note: The party paper announced a shield for peace; the Stasi counted crowds, a 'KZ' remark and approval it partly supplied; Brandt, back from the campaign trail, called the measures unlawful and asked his city for calm. Each wrote for a different audience, and none of them for the people at the wire.

convergences.label: Third day: the guard who jumps, the West that waits
convergences.note: In the afternoon one of the new border's guards left it in a single leap. The Stasi's report of the same day told the leadership that the West Berlin mayor and the commandants had agreed to avoid provocation.

convergences.label: Letters and headlines
convergences.note: Brandt's private letter asked Kennedy for visible action; Bild's front page accused the West of doing nothing; Grass and Schnurre asked the writers of the East to say where they stood. Three Western voices, three addressees, one complaint about silence.

convergences.label: Answers across the line
convergences.note: Within two days both open questions got answers. Hermlin told the Western writers that Berlin had been divided since 1948; Kennedy told Brandt that only war could reverse what had happened. From opposite sides, both said the line was a fact.

convergences.label: Johnson and Clay in Berlin; the battle group on the autobahn
convergences.note: Kennedy's reply arrived with the men it announced. Johnson's pledge and the troops' arrival answered Brandt's request for a visible sign, and Johnson's own report noted that the crowd cheered the tanks loudest.

convergences.label: Bernauer Straße 48
convergences.note: The East Berlin log noted a jump from No. 48 in a few lines, as 'a man', between crowd counts and motorcades; the Western papers named Ida Siekmann and called her death a jump to freedom. Brandt and Adenauer came to the same street that day and were logged by the police across the line.

convergences.label: The first shooting
convergences.note: The Transportpolizei wrote of a prevented border breakthrough; the East Berlin press of a criminal who disregarded warning shots; the West Berlin papers of murder. The family, told to keep silent, learned the truth from Western television.

convergences.label: Checkpoint Charlie
convergences.note: Clay insisted on the old four-power right to enter East Berlin without showing papers to East German police; Soviet tanks came to make clear who stood behind the GDR. The pullback the next morning is credited by different memoirs to different men.

ties.note: Brandt's letter of 16 August and Kennedy's reply of 18 August are the central exchange of the first week.
Kennedy sent Johnson to Bonn and Berlin, carrying the reply to Brandt; Johnson reported back to him.
Clay travelled with Johnson on 19–20 August and returned in September as the President's representative.
Johnson's report describes a private talk in which Brandt was apologetic about his letter.
Hermlin's letter of 17 August is a direct reply to the open letter of Grass and Schnurre of 16 August.
The police journal of 22 August records the jump from Bernauer Straße 48 without her name.
The Transportpolizei report of 24 August names Günter Litfin as the 'border violator' its men shot.
The East Berlin party press disparaged Litfin as a criminal; his family was pressed into silence.
Stasi reports to the leadership tracked Brandt's statements and his agreement with the commandants to avoid provocation.
The East Berlin police journal logged Brandt's visit to the border on 22 August at about 9:25.
The GDR government's decree and the West Berlin mayor's speech of 13 August describe the same measures as protection and as injustice.
Schumann belonged to the East German police forces holding the new line until he leapt across it.
Both died within three days at the same sector boundary of Berlin-Mitte, the first known deaths at the wall.
Both were GDR writers. Hermlin publicly backed the closure, while Reimann's diary had already recorded the cost of division within her own family.

threads_out.note: The line drawn on 13 August 1961 stood for twenty-eight years; Bernauer Straße, where Siekmann died and Schumann jumped, is now the Berlin Wall Memorial, and Checkpoint Charlie reappears in the crowds of November 1989.
The four-power occupation of Berlin, whose rights Clay insisted on at Friedrichstraße and Brandt invoked in his letter, came from the wartime zonal agreements confirmed by the Allied leaders in 1945.
Clay was military governor in the US zone after 1945, and the 1948–49 blockade that Brandt named as the only comparable crisis grew from the division of defeated Germany.

Like Berlin, Jerusalem was a city cut by an armistice line, with a single crossing point (the Mandelbaum Gate) between its halves until 1967; both chapters show neighbours living across a line one side called a border and the other refused to accept.

images.title: Residents watch the construction from the western side of Bernauer Straße
images.caption: Photograph of West Berliners watching the border being sealed on Bernauer Straße, where the house fronts stood in the East and the pavement in the West. It is the street of Ida Siekmann's and Conrad Schumann's stories.

images.title: The Leap – 1961 (Deutsches Historisches Museum)
images.caption: The museum's page on Conrad Schumann's jump at Ruppiner and Bernauer Straße at 4 p.m. on 15 August 1961, photographed by Peter Leibing. The installation retells the moment from the guard's, the photographer's and a West Berlin policeman's points of view.
images.credit: Deutsches Historisches Museum; photograph Peter Leibing

images.title: Erich Mielke's photo album of the wall's construction
images.caption: A page from the album of photographs of the border closure kept by the Minister for State Security. It shows the wall as its builders chose to record it.
